title: Political Philosophy: Justice, Rights, and the State

questions.question: According to Hobbes, why would rational individuals submit to a near-absolute sovereign?
options: To express the general will of the people
To protect property rights against taxation
To escape the war of all against all and secure basic order
To guarantee free elections every five years
questions.rationale: In Hobbes' state of nature life is 'nasty, brutish, and short', so rational people trade nearly all liberty to a sovereign in exchange for peace and security.

questions.question: Locke argues that legitimate government exists to:
options: Maximise the total welfare of society
Protect natural rights to life, liberty, and property — and may be overthrown if it fails
Enforce the teachings of the established church
Abolish all private property
questions.rationale: For Locke government is a limited trust: it exists to secure pre-existing natural rights, and the people retain a right of revolution when it betrays that trust.

questions.question: For Rousseau, laws are legitimate when they express:
options: The general will of the people as a whole
The commands of an absolute monarch
A contract between rich and poor
The customs of the oldest families
questions.rationale: Rousseau grounds sovereignty in the general will: citizens obey laws they collectively author, so obedience is self-rule rather than subjection.

questions.question: Rawls' difference principle permits social and economic inequalities only when they:
options: Maximise average income
Reward the naturally talented
Benefit the least advantaged members of society
Are approved by a majority vote
questions.rationale: Behind the veil of ignorance you would allow inequalities only if they improve the position of the worst off — insuring yourself against being among them.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes negative from positive liberty?
options: Negative liberty is freedom from interference; positive liberty is the effective capability to act
Negative liberty applies to states; positive liberty applies to individuals
Negative liberty is political; positive liberty is only economic
Negative liberty means obeying nature; positive liberty means obeying the sovereign
questions.rationale: Berlin's distinction: negative liberty asks 'who stops me?', positive liberty asks 'can I actually do it?' — rights on paper versus real power to use them.

questions.question: Mill's harm principle holds that society may coerce an individual only:
options: When the majority's welfare requires it
When it is for the individual's own good
When the individual's conduct gives offence
To prevent harm to others
questions.rationale: For Mill the only justified ground for coercion is preventing harm to others; paternalism and mere offence do not qualify.

questions.question: What distinguishes a natural right from a legal right?
options: Natural rights are granted by legislatures; legal rights are not
Natural rights are claimed to hold by reason of humanity, independent of enactment; legal rights exist only by statute
Legal rights always override natural rights
Natural rights apply only to citizens
questions.rationale: A natural right (like freedom of conscience) is argued to exist even where suppressed; a legal right (like a parking entitlement) exists only because the law says so.

questions.question: Which of the following is one of Rawls' principles of justice?
options: Maximise the growth of national wealth
Strict equality of outcome for all citizens
Fair equality of opportunity for offices and positions
Merit without regard to social conditions
questions.rationale: Rawls' second principle combines fair equality of opportunity with the difference principle; he is not a strict egalitarian and does not rank raw growth first.

questions.question: Which sequence matches the values promised in the Preamble of the Indian Constitution?
options: Liberty, Justice, Equality, Fraternity
Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity
Equality, Fraternity, Justice, Liberty
Fraternity, Equality, Liberty, Justice
questions.rationale: The Preamble secures Justice (social, economic, political), Liberty (of thought, expression, belief, faith, worship), Equality (of status and opportunity), and Fraternity — dignity and unity.

questions.question: The distinction between a federal and a unitary state concerns:
options: Who rules — democracy versus autocracy
How many citizens the state has
How power is distributed between central and regional governments
Whether the state has an official religion
questions.rationale: Federal versus unitary is the structural axis of power-sharing, separate from the axis of who rules — a federal state can be authoritarian and a unitary state democratic.
